text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- The Social Democrats and conservative People's Party, which govern together at national level, have agreed to form a coalition on Vienna city council.
- President Thomas Klestil will be fit again in six months at the earliest, doctors say.
- Austrian retailers fear lower profits in the run-up to Christmas this year because they expect shoppers to spend less due to public spending cuts.
- Helmut Kramer, head of economic research institute WIFO, said European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) should be delayed if European economies are not strong enough.
- Trade union president Fritz Verzetnitsch said a maximum unemployment rate of seven percent should be introduced as another criteria for EMU.
- Steelmaker Boehler-Uddeholm's pre-tax profits fell nearly eight percent to 890 million schillings in the first nine months of 1996.
- Fibremaker Lenzing is expecting losses for 1996. However, about 500 job cuts over the next two to three years should save the company up to 600 million schillings a year.
- OMV has promised a dividend at least ten schillings higher than last year as this year's nine-month results are better than last year's.
DIE PRESSE
- Foreign minister Wolfgang Schuessel has said a concept for Austrian security policy will be prepared by mid-1997.
- Austrians consider unemployment in the European Union a major issue. The European Parliament is said to be of significant importance for two-thirds of the country's population.
- Inflation went up to 2.1 percent in October from two percent in September.
- Brewer Brau Union has stepped out of the consortium around EA-Generali bidding for Creditanstalt.
- Austrian exports to the emerging markets went down 2.6 percent in the first half of 1996.
KURIER
- State-owned telephone monopoly Post & Telekom Austria will raise prices for local calls by up to 30 percent next year, while reducing costs for long-distance calls by a similar margin.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Norwegian pharmaceuticals giant Nycomed will close down its plant in Belgium next year and at the same time will expand production in its Upper Austrian plant.
